questions.title: The exception among neural crest derivatives
questions.question: Which of the following isn't derived from the neural crest?

explanations.A: Correct. Oligodendrocytes, the CNS myelinating glia, arise from the neuroepithelium of the neural tube, not the neural crest. The exception among these four options.
explanations.B: This IS a neural-crest derivative, so it is not the answer: the pia mater (leptomeninges) derives from neural crest mesenchyme.
explanations.C: This IS a neural-crest derivative, so it is not the answer: Schwann cells, the PNS's myelinating glia, are classic neural-crest derivatives, unlike their CNS counterpart oligodendrocytes.
explanations.D: This IS a neural-crest derivative, so it is not the answer: pharyngeal-arch ectomesenchyme (cartilage, bone, connective tissue of the head and neck) derives substantially from neural crest cells.

questions.subtopic: Neural crest vs neural tube derivatives
questions.learning_objective: State that oligodendrocytes are neural-tube (not neural-crest) derivatives, unlike Schwann cells, pia mater and pharyngeal-arch mesenchyme.

questions.title: The true statement about primary motor and sensory cortex
questions.question: Regarding the cortical areas of the cerebral hemisphere, which of the following is true?

options.A: The premotor area is present in the postcentral gyrus
options.B: Astereognosis occurs due to injury of the primary auditory area
options.C: Broca's area is the sensory speech area
options.D: In both the primary motor and primary sensory areas the body is represented upside-down

explanations.A: Incorrect. The premotor area lies anterior to the precentral (primary motor) gyrus, in the frontal lobe — not in the postcentral (primary sensory) gyrus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Astereognosis results from a primary SOMATOSENSORY area (S1, postcentral gyrus) lesion, not the primary auditory area, which instead relates to hearing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) is the EXPRESSIVE (motor) speech area; Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) is the sensory (receptive) speech area.
explanations.D: Correct. In both the precentral (primary motor) and postcentral (primary sensory) gyri, the somatotopic map is inverted: the leg and foot are represented superiorly (extending onto the medial surface), the trunk and arm at the mid-convexity, and the face/hand inferiorly and laterally near the Sylvian fissure. A shared inversion of BOTH primary areas.

questions.learning_objective: State that both the primary motor and primary sensory cortex represent the body upside-down.

questions.title: Structure labelled B — ciliary body and accommodation
questions.question: Which of the following statements describes the structure labelled B in the figure below?

options.A: It is involved in the regulation of accommodation
options.B: It is the site of outflow of vitreous humor from the posterior chamber
options.C: It is responsible for the production of aqueous humor
options.D: It is the site of blockage in glaucoma

explanations.A: Correct. The structure labelled B is the ciliary body, which, via the ciliary muscle acting through the zonular fibers on the lens capsule, regulates accommodation. Adjusting lens curvature/power for near vision.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aqueous humor (not vitreous humor) flows from the posterior to the anterior chamber and out via the trabecular meshwork/canal of Schlemm — a different structure and fluid from the one described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aqueous humor PRODUCTION is a function of the ciliary EPITHELIUM's secretory cells, a related but functionally distinct role from the ciliary body's own accommodation function being tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The site of blockage in (angle-closure) glaucoma is the iridocorneal angle/trabecular meshwork, not the ciliary body's accommodation-regulating function.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ciliary body as the structure regulating accommodation.

questions.title: Nerve first affected in internal carotid artery aneurysm
questions.question: Which of the following nerves is firstly affected in case of internal carotid artery aneurysm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve runs in the cavernous sinus's LATERAL dural wall, like the trochlear and ophthalmic/maxillary divisions, and is not the first affected.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The trochlear nerve likewise runs in the lateral dural wall, embedded in dura rather than freely within the venous cavity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The maxillary nerve (V2) also runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not freely within it.
explanations.D: Correct. The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique among the nerves related to the cavernous sinus in running freely within the venous cavity itself, immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery, rather than within the sinus's lateral dural wall. Which is why it is the cranial nerve most vulnerable to compression from cavernous sinus pathology such as an internal carotid artery aneurysm.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the abducens nerve as the cranial nerve most vulnerable to internal carotid artery/cavernous sinus pathology.

questions.title: Occlusion in neuronal pool integration
questions.question: Which of the following is related to occlusion?

options.A: Due to stimulation of two afferent neurons away from each other
options.B: Occurs when two afferent neurons shared a common discharge zone
options.C: Results in a greater response than if each afferent neuron is stimulated alone
options.D: Occurs when two afferent neurons shared a common facilitated zone

explanations.A: Incorrect. Two afferents stimulated far away from each other, with no overlapping neuronal pool, would produce simple additive summation, not the convergence occlusion requires.
explanations.B: Correct. Occlusion is a spinal integrative phenomenon in which two afferent inputs converge on an overlapping (shared) pool of postsynaptic neurons, so their combined response is LESS than the arithmetic sum of each input's individual response, because some of the same neurons are already being fired by both inputs. This is why a clinician cannot simply add up the expected effect of two separate reflex-triggering stimuli when they are known to recruit an overlapping spinal neuronal pool.
explanations.C: Incorrect — reversed. Occlusion produces a LESS-than-additive (not greater) combined response; a greater-than-additive response instead describes facilitation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A shared subliminal FACILITATED zone (neurons brought near but not to threshold by either input alone) describes facilitation, the opposite integrative phenomenon from occlusion's shared, already-discharging zone.

questions.learning_objective: State that occlusion occurs when two afferent neurons share a common discharge zone, producing a less-than-additive response.

questions.title: Definition of a ganglion
questions.question: Which of the following defines a ganglion?

options.A: Group of nerve fibers with same origin, end & function
options.B: Group of close nerve cells with same function inside CNS
options.C: Group of nerve fibers with different origin, end & function
options.D: Group of close nerve cells with same function outside CNS

explanations.A: Incorrect. A group of nerve FIBERS sharing origin, course and function (inside or outside the CNS) is a tract or nerve, not a ganglion, which is defined by cell bodies, not fibers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A group of nerve CELL BODIES sharing function INSIDE the CNS is a nucleus, not a ganglion, which is specifically an extra-CNS structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This does not describe a coherent anatomical grouping at all (fibers of different origin/end/function are not organised as a named structure), and fibers regardless are not what defines a ganglion.
explanations.D: Correct. By definition, a ganglion is a cluster of neuron CELL BODIES (not fibers) located OUTSIDE the CNS — for example dorsal root ganglia (sensory) or autonomic ganglia. Distinguishing it from an intra-CNS nucleus (cell bodies) or a tract/nerve (fibers).

questions.learning_objective: State that a ganglion is a group of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS.

questions.title: Sixth pharyngeal arch derivative
questions.question: Which of the following is derived from the sixth pharyngeal arch?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cricothyroid is instead classically taught as a fourth-arch (superior laryngeal nerve) muscle, distinct from the sixth arch's own intrinsic laryngeal muscles (supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve).
explanations.B: Correct. The sixth pharyngeal arch cartilage forms the arytenoid, cricoid and corniculate cartilages of the larynx. The recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus (the sixth arch's own nerve), supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles these cartilages anchor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thyroid cartilage derives from the FOURTH arch, not the sixth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The greater horn of the hyoid bone derives from the THIRD arch, not the sixth.

questions.learning_objective: State that the arytenoid cartilage is a sixth-arch derivative.

questions.title: Mechanism of enkephalin's block of pain transmission
questions.question: Enkephalin blocks pain transmission by:

options.A: Blocking the response of pain receptors to painful stimuli
options.B: Slowing down transmission of pain impulses through synapses in the pain pathway
options.C: Inhibiting the response of the cerebral cortical somatic sensory area to pain signals
options.D: Blocking Ca2+ channels in the central terminals of pain sensory fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. Enkephalin acts centrally at the dorsal horn synapse, not peripherally on the pain receptor's own response to a painful stimulus.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the specific mechanism — enkephalin does more than generically 'slow' transmission; it acts via a specific presynaptic Ca2+-channel-blocking mechanism (option D).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enkephalin acts at the spinal (dorsal horn) level, not at the cerebral cortex.
explanations.D: Correct. Enkephalin, an endogenous opioid released by inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, binds presynaptic opioid receptors on the central terminals of primary nociceptive afferents, closing voltage-gated Ca2+ channels there, reducing Ca2+ influx and hence neurotransmitter release onto the second-order (transmission) neuron. A presynaptic inhibitory mechanism.

questions.learning_objective: State that enkephalin inhibits pain transmission presynaptically, by blocking Ca2+ channels in nociceptive afferent central terminals.

questions.title: Degeneration of the inner-ear structure and neural deafness
questions.question: In the figure, degeneration of the structure pointed out by the arrow in the inner ear of a patient causes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Motion sickness relates to vestibular (not cochlear) mismatch signalling, not degeneration of the cochlear hair cells.
explanations.B: Correct. Degeneration of the cochlear (organ of Corti) hair cells, or of the cochlear nerve fibers relaying their signal, produces sensorineural hearing loss. Described in older terminology as 'neural' deafness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vertigo results from vestibular (semicircular canal/otolith) rather than cochlear pathology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conductive deafness results from a problem in the external/middle ear's sound-conducting mechanism (ossicles, tympanic membrane) with an intact cochlea and nerve — the opposite mechanism from the cochlear degeneration pictured here.

questions.subtopic: Hair cell degeneration and hearing loss
questions.learning_objective: State that degeneration of cochlear hair cells causes sensorineural (neural) deafness.

questions.title: Nuclei of the lateral horns of grey matter
questions.question: The lateral horns of grey matter contain which of the following nuclei?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 'Commissural' is not a recognised named nucleus of spinal grey matter; it describes fibers crossing the midline, not a lateral-horn cell column.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Motor (somatic efferent) nuclei occupy the ANTERIOR horn, not the lateral horn.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sensory relay nuclei occupy the POSTERIOR horn, not the lateral horn.
explanations.D: Correct. The lateral horn, present at thoracic/upper lumbar (T1-L2) and sacral (S2-4) segments, contains the intermediolateral cell column. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons at T1-L2 and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons at S2-4.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral horn of spinal grey matter houses autonomic (sympathetic/parasympathetic) preganglionic nuclei.

questions.title: Tract exiting via the inferior cerebellar peduncle
questions.question: Which of the following tracts exit from the inferior cerebellar peduncle?

explanations.A: Correct. The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries a genuine EFFERENT component leaving the cerebellum. Including cerebello-vestibular and cerebello-reticular fibers, projecting from the fastigial nucleus to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation respectively.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A cerebello-olivary projection is not the efferent tract classically named as exiting via the inferior peduncle; the olivocerebellar tract instead runs the OPPOSITE (afferent, INTO the cerebellum) direction via this same peduncle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Corticopontocerebellar fibers ENTER the cerebellum via the MIDDLE cerebellar peduncle, which is purely afferent, not the inferior peduncle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vestibulocerebellar fibers largely travel INTO the cerebellum (afferent) via the inferior peduncle; the efferent direction being tested here is instead the cerebello-vestibular/cerebello-reticular projection.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cerebello-reticular tract as an efferent pathway leaving the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.title: Basilar membrane amplitude and loudness
questions.question: Which of the following events makes the auditory system interpret a sound as loud?

options.A: Fewer inner hair cells are stimulated
options.B: Hair cells excite nerve endings at a diminished rate
options.C: Amplitude of vibration of the basilar membrane decreases
options.D: Amplitude of vibration of the basilar membrane increases

explanations.A: Incorrect — reversed. A louder sound recruits MORE, not fewer, stimulated hair cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect — reversed. A louder sound causes hair cells to excite nerve endings at an INCREASED, not diminished, rate.
explanations.C: Incorrect — reversed. Decreased basilar membrane vibration amplitude would signal a SOFTER, not louder, sound.
explanations.D: Correct. Loudness perception is coded by the amplitude of basilar membrane vibration at a given frequency's characteristic place. A louder sound produces a larger-amplitude traveling wave, deflecting more hair cell stereocilia more strongly and increasing their firing rate.

questions.learning_objective: State that increased basilar membrane vibration amplitude codes for increased loudness.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p4 q12, answer table p10

questions.title: The Y-shaped sheet dividing the thalamus
questions.question: The Y-shaped sheet of white matter that divides the thalamus into its three main parts (anterior, medial, and lateral) is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lamina terminalis is a separate midline diencephalic structure (part of the anterior wall of the third ventricle), not an intrathalamic dividing sheet.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The stria medullaris thalami is a fiber bundle on the thalamus's dorsomedial surface, not an internal dividing sheet.
explanations.C: Correct. The internal medullary lamina is a Y-shaped sheet of myelinated fibers within the thalamus that partitions its grey matter into the anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups, splitting anteriorly to enclose the anterior nuclear group. The lamina's Y-shape also encloses a nucleus of its own significance, the intralaminar nuclei, involved in arousal and consciousness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lamina cribrosa refers to perforated structures elsewhere (e.g. the optic nerve head or renal pelvis), not a thalamic dividing sheet.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the internal medullary lamina as the Y-shaped fiber sheet dividing the thalamus into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups.

questions.title: The exception among cochlear duct characteristics
questions.question: The cochlear duct isn't characterized by which of the following?

options.A: It communicates with the middle ear through the round window
options.C: It represents the membranous part of the cochlea
options.D: It is present between the scala tympani and scala vestibuli

explanations.A: Correct. This is the exception. The cochlear duct (scala media) is a closed compartment that does NOT open directly into the middle ear; the round window instead lies at the basal end of the perilymph-filled scala tympani, separated from the middle ear by the secondary tympanic membrane.
explanations.B: This DOES characterise the cochlear duct, so it is not the answer: it is filled with endolymph, unlike the perilymph-filled scalae on either side.
explanations.C: This DOES characterise the cochlear duct, so it is not the answer: it is indeed the membranous (endolymph-filled) part of the cochlea.
explanations.D: This DOES characterise the cochlear duct, so it is not the answer: it lies between the scala vestibuli and scala tympani, exactly as described.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cochlear duct does not communicate with the middle ear via the round window.

questions.title: Artery sharing in the supply of the medulla
questions.question: The following artery shares in the supply of the medulla:

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), typically a branch of the vertebral artery, supplies the dorsolateral medulla (along with the inferior cerebellar surface). Its occlusion produces the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior cerebellar artery, a branch of the basilar artery, supplies the pons/midbrain and superior cerebellum, not the medulla.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital and inferomedial temporal lobes and the thalamus, not the medulla.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral cerebral hemisphere, an entirely different (anterior circulation, cerebral) territory from the medulla.

questions.learning_objective: State that the posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the medulla.

questions.title: Muscle spindle responsiveness during contraction
questions.question: The muscle spindle remains capable of responding to stretch even while the muscle is contracting. This is because of:

options.A: Presence of stretch receptors in the tendon
options.B: Co-activation of alpha- and gamma-motor neurons

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stretch receptors in the TENDON (the Golgi tendon organ) signal tension, not spindle stretch sensitivity, and would not by themselves keep the spindle itself responsive.
explanations.B: Correct. During a voluntary contraction, the central nervous system drives alpha and gamma motor neurons together (co-activation): as alpha discharge shortens the extrafusal fibers, parallel gamma discharge takes up the corresponding slack in the spindle's own intrafusal fibers, keeping the spindle taut and sensitive to any additional stretch. Without this parallel gamma drive the spindle would fall slack and go silent as the muscle shortens.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reciprocal innervation describes simultaneous inhibition of an antagonist muscle during agonist contraction, an unrelated spinal circuit from the spindle's own stretch sensitivity during contraction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Autogenic inhibition is the Golgi tendon organ's inhibitory action on the SAME muscle's alpha motor neurons, not the mechanism keeping the spindle responsive to stretch.

questions.learning_objective: State that alpha-gamma co-activation keeps the muscle spindle responsive to stretch throughout an active contraction.

questions.title: Structure detecting angular deceleration
questions.question: Which of the following is related to the structure shown in the figure?

options.B: Considered the neuroepithelial thickening in the utricle

explanations.A: Incorrect per this fact pattern — a structure covered by the tectorial membrane is the organ of Corti (hearing), not the pictured vestibular structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect — a neuroepithelial thickening within the utricle describes the macula of the utricle (linear acceleration/head position), a different vestibular receptor from the one pictured here.
explanations.C: Incorrect — pillar cells are a feature of the organ of Corti (hearing), not this vestibular structure.
explanations.D: Correct. The crista ampullaris, a sensory ridge within each semicircular canal's ampulla, is covered by a gelatinous cupula that deflects with endolymph flow during head rotation, exciting hair cells to signal angular acceleration/deceleration. The structure the figure depicts.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the crista ampullaris as the structure that detects angular acceleration/deceleration.

questions.title: Muscle bending the head to the same side, rotating to the opposite
questions.question: What is the muscle responsible for bending the head to the same side and rotating the face to the opposite side?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trapezius chiefly produces shoulder shrug and scapular rotation, not the combined head-tilt/face-rotation action described.
explanations.B: Correct. Unilateral contraction of sternocleidomastoid produces lateral flexion (bending) of the head toward the SAME side as the contracting muscle, combined with rotation of the face toward the OPPOSITE side. This combined action is exploited clinically to test spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) function at the bedside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Scalenus medius chiefly elevates the first rib and laterally flexes the neck, without the same combined rotary action as sternocleidomastoid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression (cheek compression), unrelated to head movement.

questions.learning_objective: State that sternocleidomastoid produces ipsilateral head tilt with contralateral face rotation.

questions.title: Functional component of the accessory nerve nucleus
questions.question: What is the type of the cranial nucleus responsible for the formation of the nerve referred to above (the accessory nerve supplying sternocleidomastoid)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. GSE (general somatic efferent) describes nuclei like the oculomotor or hypoglossal, supplying non-branchial-arch (myotome-derived) muscle, not the accessory nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GVE (general visceral efferent) describes autonomic (parasympathetic) motor nuclei, not the accessory nerve's own skeletal-muscle motor supply.
explanations.C: Correct. The cranial nerves supplying muscles derived embryologically from the pharyngeal (branchial) arches — trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus and the cranial/spinal accessory nerve (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius). Share the SVE (special visceral efferent, branchiomotor) functional component.
explanations.D: Incorrect. SVA (special visceral afferent) is a SENSORY category (e.g. taste), not applicable to the accessory nerve's own motor function.

questions.learning_objective: State that the accessory nerve's motor nucleus is classified SVE (branchiomotor).

questions.title: The cell not attached to Purkinje cells
questions.question: Which of the following cells isn't attached to Purkinje cells?

explanations.A: This IS directly synaptically connected to Purkinje cells, so it is not the answer: basket cells synapse on the Purkinje soma/axon initial segment.
explanations.B: Incorrect per this source's own printed key, though the Golgi cell is the cell most commonly taught as NOT synapsing directly on Purkinje cells (it mainly targets granule cell dendrites in the granular layer's glomeruli instead) — see this concept's field_notes.
explanations.C: This IS directly synaptically connected to Purkinje cells, so it is not the answer: granule cells, via their parallel-fiber axons, synapse directly on Purkinje cell dendritic spines.
explanations.D: Correct per this source's own printed answer key. Note: stellate cells are widely taught as forming direct axo-dendritic synapses onto Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer, which would instead make the Golgi cell (option B) — whose synapses target granule cell dendrites in the granular layer, not the Purkinje cell — the more commonly taught exception. This source's own answer table nonetheless marks D; see this concept's field_notes for the discrepancy.

questions.learning_objective: State this source's own printed answer for the cerebellar interneuron not attached to Purkinje cells, and recognise the standard Golgi-cell alternative.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p6 q20, answer table p10
questions.author_notes: keySource: printed answer table p10. Doubt: the source's key (D, stellate cell) conflicts with standard cerebellar histology, which instead treats the Golgi cell (option B) as the interneuron not directly synapsing on Purkinje cells (it targets granule cell dendrites instead), with stellate cells forming genuine direct Purkinje-dendrite synapses. Printed key kept per LANE-CARD; doubt recorded here and in the concept's field_notes.

questions.title: Mechanism of gate theory pain suppression
questions.question: Upon which mechanism is "the gate theory of pain suppression" based?

explanations.A: Correct per this source's own printed key. In the gate-control theory, large-diameter A-beta tactile afferents excite inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa, which in turn inhibit the dorsal-horn transmission (T) cell that relays nociceptive input onward; because this interneuron-to-transmission-cell synapse is itself a conventional postsynaptic inhibitory synapse, this framing describes the mechanism at that specific relay as postsynaptic inhibition of the transmission cell. This is the same substantia-gelatinosa circuit the gate theory's fiber-type question (large A-beta afferents) draws on, viewed here from its synaptic mechanism rather than its afferent trigger.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The gate theory operates at the spinal cord's own dorsal horn, not by a generic 'brain-level' pain block.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A brain opiate (endogenous analgesia) system is a related but distinct mechanism from the gate theory's own spinal dorsal-horn circuit.
explanations.D: Incorrect per this source's own printed key, though many teaching sources instead frame the gate theory's tactile-afferent inhibition as acting presynaptically on the nociceptive afferent's own terminal — see this concept's field_notes for the fuller picture of both framings.

questions.learning_objective: State that gate-theory pain suppression operates through inhibitory dorsal-horn interneurons acting on the transmission (T) cell.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p7 q21, answer table p10
questions.author_notes: keySource: printed answer table p10. Several teaching sources instead frame the gate theory's mechanism as presynaptic inhibition of the nociceptive afferent terminal itself (option D); both framings describe the same substantia-gelatinosa interneuron circuit from slightly different synaptic vantage points, so this is treated as a defensible convention rather than a clear error — see the concept's own definition. contextual_concept_ids links the sibling gate-theory fiber-type concept (Quiz 2 Q25, CON-NEU-04F9C773D465DB).

questions.title: Blood supply of the precuneus gyrus
questions.question: What is the blood supply of the precuneus gyrus?

explanations.A: Incorrect per this source's own printed key, though the precuneus does sit in an anterior/posterior cerebral artery border zone, with some texts also crediting the PCA.
explanations.B: Correct. The precuneus, on the medial surface of the parietal lobe between the marginal (cingulate) sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus, is most often attributed in standard vascular-territory teaching to the pericallosal/distal branches of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA). This border-zone position also makes the precuneus a classic site of watershed infarction in severe hypotension.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The middle cerebral artery supplies the LATERAL cerebral convexity, not the medial parietal surface where the precuneus sits.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vertebral artery supplies posterior fossa/brainstem structures, not the cerebral hemisphere's medial parietal cortex.

questions.learning_objective: State that the precuneus's blood supply is chiefly attributed to the anterior cerebral artery.

questions.title: The exception among corticospinal tract disease features
questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of corticospinal tract disease?

explanations.A: Correct. Cogwheel rigidity is a basal ganglia (extrapyramidal, e.g. Parkinsonian) sign, reflecting a fundamentally different motor system's dysfunction, and is not a feature of corticospinal tract (pyramidal) disease.
explanations.B: This IS a feature of corticospinal tract disease, so it is not the answer: spasticity is a classic upper motor neuron sign.
explanations.C: This IS a feature of corticospinal tract disease, so it is not the answer: an extensor plantar (Babinski) response is a classic upper motor neuron sign.
explanations.D: This IS a feature of corticospinal tract disease, so it is not the answer: exaggerated deep tendon reflexes are a classic upper motor neuron sign.

questions.learning_objective: State that cogwheel rigidity is an extrapyramidal (basal ganglia) sign, not a feature of corticospinal tract disease.

questions.title: Definition of after-discharge
questions.question: Which of the following is related to after-discharge?

options.A: Is decreased response with maintained stimulus
options.B: Is increased response with maintained stimulus
options.C: Is maintained response after stoppage of stimulus

explanations.A: Incorrect. A decreased response during a maintained stimulus describes adaptation, not after-discharge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An increased response during a maintained stimulus describes facilitation/summation during ongoing stimulation, not after-discharge's defining feature of outlasting the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct. After-discharge describes continued neuronal firing that outlasts the triggering stimulus, typically produced by reverberating (recurrent, self-re-exciting) neural circuits or prolonged synaptic potentials, so the response persists after stimulation has stopped. A classic example is the prolonged reflex activity seen after a single strong afferent volley in some spinal reflex circuits.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While reverberating (closed-chain) circuits are one common mechanism producing after-discharge, after-discharge itself is defined by its persistence after stimulus cessation, not by requiring only a closed-chain circuit specifically.

questions.learning_objective: State that after-discharge is a maintained response persisting after stimulus cessation.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p7 q24, answer table p10

questions.title: Most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter
questions.question: What is the most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter?

explanations.A: Incorrect. GABA is the CNS's principal INHIBITORY, not excitatory, neurotransmitter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) are widely used but are not the CNS's most abundant excitatory transmitter overall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acetylcholine, though an important excitatory transmitter at the neuromuscular junction and in some CNS circuits, is not the most abundant CNS excitatory transmitter.
explanations.D: Correct. Glutamate is the CNS's principal and most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter, acting on ionotropic (AMPA, NMDA, kainate) and metabotropic receptors throughout the brain and spinal cord. Excess glutamatergic activity, conversely, is implicated in excitotoxic neuronal injury following ischemic stroke.

questions.learning_objective: State that glutamate is the CNS's most abundant excitatory neurotransmitter.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p7 q25, answer table p10

questions.title: Nerve supplying sensation to the upper last molar
questions.question: A 23-year-old male presents with toothache in the upper last molar teeth. Which of the following nerves is responsible for transmission of this sensation?

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior superior alveolar nerve, a branch of the maxillary nerve (V2), supplies sensory innervation to the maxillary molar teeth (most reliably the second and third/'last' molars) and the overlying gingiva and maxillary sinus mucosa. Because these roots lie close to the maxillary sinus floor, upper molar infections can also spread to cause sinusitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the incisors and canine, not the last molar.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior alveolar nerve (V3) supplies the LOWER (mandibular) teeth, not the upper molars.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the premolars and the first molar's mesiobuccal root (when present), not the last (third) molar.

questions.learning_objective: State that the posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies sensation to the upper molar teeth.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p8 q26, answer table p10

questions.title: The true statement about endolymph
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the endolymph?

options.A: Is found within the membranous labyrinth
options.B: Has a K+ concentration similar to the extracellular fluid
options.C: Bathes the bases of the hair cells of the organ of Corti
options.D: Is electrically negative with respect to perilymph

explanations.A: Correct. Endolymph fills the entire membranous labyrinth. The cochlear duct (scala media), utricle, saccule and semicircular ducts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endolymph has an unusually HIGH potassium (and low sodium) concentration, more like intracellular than typical extracellular fluid — not similar to ordinary extracellular fluid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Endolymph bathes the APICAL surfaces (stereocilia) of the hair cells, not their bases, which sit within a different perilymph-like compartment (cortilymph) inside the organ of Corti.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Endolymph is electrically POSITIVE (the endocochlear potential, roughly +80mV) relative to perilymph, not negative.

questions.learning_objective: State that endolymph fills the membranous labyrinth and is high in K+, unlike typical extracellular fluid.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p8 q27, answer table p10

questions.title: Substance at higher concentration in CSF than plasma
questions.question: Which of the following substances is found at a higher concentration in CSF than in plasma?

explanations.A: Incorrect. CSF urea is similar to or slightly lower than plasma urea, not higher.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CSF protein is markedly LOWER than plasma protein, reflecting the blood-CSF barrier's restriction of large plasma proteins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CSF calcium is lower than plasma (total) calcium.
explanations.D: Correct. Folate is actively transported across the choroid plexus by folate receptors, resulting in a CSF folate concentration roughly three times higher than plasma folate. A genuine exception among substances compared between the two fluids.

questions.learning_objective: State that folate, unlike urea, protein or calcium, is present at a higher concentration in CSF than in plasma.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p8 q28, answer table p10

questions.title: Origin of the artery passing in the basilar sulcus
questions.question: What is the origin of the artery passing in this sulcus (figure)?

explanations.A: Correct. The basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction, runs along the midline basilar sulcus on the pons's ventral surface, giving off paramedian and short/long circumferential branches that supply the pons. Occlusion of these paramedian branches produces medial pontine syndromes with contralateral hemiplegia and, if the abducens nucleus/fascicle is involved, ipsilateral gaze palsy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal carotid artery is an anterior-circulation vessel supplying the cerebral hemispheres via the circle of Willis, not the vessel running in the pons's own midline groove.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The external carotid artery supplies extracranial head and neck structures, not the brainstem.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid artery, supplies the tongue, unrelated to any brainstem sulcus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the artery running in the pons's basilar sulcus is the basilar artery.

questions.title: Mechanism of the mass reflex
questions.question: Which of the following is related to the mass reflex?

options.A: Is a sign of a central inhibitory state
options.C: Is due to irradiation of afferent impulses
options.D: Is a manifestation of 'release of spinal reflexes' from stimulatory control by higher centers

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mass reflex reflects a state of exaggerated, disinhibited excitability, not a central INHIBITORY state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mass reflex is a feature of chronic (post-shock) spinal cord injury with an isolated cord below the lesion, not the acute decerebrate preparation.
explanations.C: Correct. After spinal shock resolves in a chronic spinal cord injury, a mild stimulus below the lesion can trigger a widespread, exaggerated response because the stimulus's afferent impulses IRRADIATE (spread widely) through many spinal cord segments isolated from higher control, recruiting far more neurons than the same stimulus would in an intact cord. Because it signals recovering (rather than absent) spinal reflex activity, the mass reflex's re-emergence is often welcomed clinically as evidence that spinal shock has resolved.
explanations.D: Incorrect as stated. The mass reflex arises from release of spinal reflexes from higher centers' INHIBITORY (not stimulatory) control — losing inhibition, not losing excitatory drive, is what disinhibits the exaggerated response.

questions.learning_objective: State that the mass reflex arises from irradiation of afferent impulses within the isolated (chronically injured) spinal cord.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p9 q30, answer table p10

questions.title: Most lateral nucleus in the cerebellar white matter
questions.question: Which of the following is considered the most lateral nucleus in the white matter of the cerebellum?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fastigial nucleus is the most MEDIAL of the four deep cerebellar nuclei, not the most lateral.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The emboliform nucleus lies between the globose and dentate nuclei, not at the most lateral position.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The globose nucleus, together with the emboliform, forms the intermediate ('interposed') nuclear group, not the most lateral nucleus.
explanations.D: Correct. The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral of the four deep cerebellar nuclei (fastigial, globose, emboliform, dentate, medial to lateral), embedded in the cerebellar medulla (white matter). Its efferent fibers project chiefly via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus, supporting the planning of skilled voluntary movement.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dentate nucleus is the most lateral of the four deep cerebellar nuclei.

questions.title: Primary cutaneous hyperalgesia
questions.question: Primary cutaneous hyperalgesia:

options.A: Develops in the normal skin region around the area of flare
options.B: Is an abnormal condition in the skin in which painful stimuli become more severe
options.C: Is due to changes in threshold of pain receptors
options.D: Is associated with a throbbing type of pain

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperalgesia developing in the normal skin surrounding the area of flare describes SECONDARY, not primary, hyperalgesia.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the best-characterising statement — this vague description does not identify the specific PERIPHERAL mechanism (receptor threshold change) that defines primary hyperalgesia, which option C names directly.
explanations.C: Correct. Primary hyperalgesia occurs directly within the injured tissue, where local inflammatory mediators sensitize nociceptors, lowering their activation threshold so normally mild stimuli become painful. Secondary hyperalgesia in the surrounding normal skin, by contrast, results from central (dorsal horn) sensitization rather than a change in the peripheral receptors themselves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A throbbing pain quality is not the specific defining feature of primary hyperalgesia, which is instead defined by its peripheral receptor-threshold mechanism and its location within the injured tissue itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that primary cutaneous hyperalgesia results from a lowered peripheral pain-receptor threshold in the injured tissue itself.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p9 q32, answer table p10

questions.title: Location of the substantia nigra
questions.question: The substantia nigra is present in which of the following sites?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The substantia nigra does not span into the pons; it is confined to the midbrain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medulla oblongata is well below the substantia nigra's actual (midbrain) location.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer — the substantia nigra is not confined only to the SUPERIOR midbrain; it extends throughout the midbrain's length, making the broader 'midbrain' answer the more complete and accurate choice.
explanations.D: Correct. The substantia nigra, a dopaminergic nucleus of the basal ganglia system, is located throughout the midbrain (mesencephalon), extending from its upper to lower limits. Its degeneration underlies Parkinson disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that the substantia nigra is a midbrain structure, spanning its extent.
questions.source_citation: AU-MED-203 Workshop Quiz 4, p9 q33, answer table p10

questions.title: Cause of decreased CSF sugar
questions.question: Which of the following causes a decrease in CSF sugar?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A traumatic tap introduces blood into the CSF sample but does not itself lower true CSF glucose.
explanations.B: Incorrect per this source's own printed key, though bacterial meningitis is the condition most standardly taught to cause LOW CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia), via glucose consumption by bacteria and infiltrating leukocytes.
explanations.C: Correct per this source's own printed answer key. Note: standard clinical teaching instead attributes low CSF glucose specifically to bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis (option B), with viral meningitis and encephalitis classically showing a NORMAL CSF glucose — a distinction used clinically to differentiate bacterial from viral CNS infection. This source's own answer table nonetheless marks C; see this concept's field_notes for the discrepancy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Jaundice (raised bilirubin) does not lower CSF glucose.

questions.learning_objective: State this source's own printed answer for the cause of decreased CSF glucose, and recognise the standard bacterial-meningitis alternative.
